titleStmt.title: Evaluating message transmission times in Controller Area Network (CAN) without buffer preemption revisited

analytic.title: Evaluating message transmission times in Controller Area Network (CAN) without buffer preemption revisited

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Controller area network (CAN) is a serial, broadcast bus, and is currently the de-facto standard for in-vehicle data transmission. CAN is the most widely used automotive communication network having the advantages of being low-cost and providing flexible and robust communication with bounded delay. CAN networks are mainly used for safety-critical real-time applications that have strict timing requirements in communication. This time-criticality makes the CAN schedulability analysis that has been studied over two decades crucial. Most of the previous studies on CAN schedulability assume an idealized communication model, with an unlimited number of transmit buffers in the communication controller.

In this paper, we address the CAN schedulability analysis for the case of a single transmit buffer without buffer preemption when the buffering overhead can be ignored. We revisit the existing worst-case response-time analysis for this case that is based on the early, flawed CAN analysis, and we present a revised schedulability analysis. Moreover, we evaluate and compare the analyses by means of example message sets.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION A. Background
div.p: Controller Area Network (CAN) [1,2] is a serial, broadcast bus that was developed by Robert Bosch GmbH in the mid-1980s and became an ISO standard in 1993. CAN has as advantages its low-cost, and flexible and robust communication with bounded delay. It is currently the defacto standard for in-vehicle data transmission.

CAN supports priority based message arbitration and non-preemptive message transmission. A standard CAN 2.0A data frame consists of seven fields: start of frame (SOF) bit, 18-bit header, 0-8 byte data, 15bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC) field, 3-bit acknowledgement slot (ACK), 7-bit end of frame field (EOF) and last 3-bit interframe space. In this paper EOF and inter-frame space fields are considered together as inter-frame time that provides the necessary time interval (10-bit time) between consecutive message frames.

Moreover, the header of a frame can be divided into 3 minor fields that are 11-bit identifier field (29-bit for CAN 2.0B, extended format), remote transmission request (RTR) bit and 4-bit data length code (DLC). The identifier part that is unique for each message defines message priorities during arbitration for the bus access. The equations to calculate the maximum CAN message length (lm) in bits are given in [3].

CAN arbitration is based on CSMA/CR (carrier sense multiple access/collision resolution), a mechanism to resolve frame collisions during transmission on the bus. Each CAN node monitors the bus and when the node detects that the bus is idle, it starts transmission beginning with the identifier field of the message. However, it is possible that other nodes in the network may start transmission at the same time. CAN arbitration procedure that lasts for the length of the identifier field defines the winner node, i.e. the node with the highest priority and, that will complete transmission without any preemption.

CAN networks are widely used for safety-critical real-time applications that have strict timing requirements in communication. This timecriticality makes the CAN communication schedulability analysis that has been studied over two decades crucial. The studies on CAN schedulabiliy analysis can roughly be examined under two headings based on the real-time communication models, i.e. the idealized and more-realistic communication models. In an idealized communication model, hardware and implementation issues [4] are neglected for the analysis, such as (i) various types of queuing of messages at nodes, e.g. first-in-first-out (FIFO) or priority-based, (ii) a limited number of transfer buffers in communication controllers, (iii) buffering overhead, i.e. the amount of time spent on refilling a transmit buffer, and (iv) buffer preemption, i.e. in case all of the transmit buffers in the CAN communication controller are occupied, the transmission of a message, awaiting in a transmit buffer to be sent, can be canceled upon a release of a higher priority message in the same node. Most of the CAN communication controllers offer buffer preemption as an implementation preference that allows the designer to implement the transmit operation with or without buffer preemption. These four issues, mentioned above, are independent parameters that are determined by the software implementation, host, and communication controller of a node.

Most of the previous studies on CAN schedulability assume an idealized communication model, with an unlimited number of transmit buffers in the communication controller. For a more realistic schedulability test of a CAN network, overheads due to hardware and implementation issues should be taken into account. Having this motivation, some previous studies address these issues, which will be explained in the following subsection. In this paper, we revisit and revise the worst-case responsetime (WCRT) analysis in [5] that addresses a single transmit buffer without buffer preemption.

div.head: B. Related Work
div.p: The schedulability analysis for CAN was first developed by Tindell et al. in 1994 [6, 7], and builds on a previous study of fixed-priority scheduling of tasks on a single processor system [8]. Davis et al. [3] showed that the existing schedulability analysis of CAN is optimistic and revised WCRT analysis for CAN. This study is complemented by [9] with formal proofs of (WCRT) analysis of tasks under fixed-priority scheduling with deferred preemption (FPDS).
Similar to most previous studies on CAN schedulability, the analysis in [3] is based on an idealized communication model.
Davis et al. [10] focussed on the issue of FIFO queues, and provide response analysis for CAN where some nodes use FIFO queues and other nodes use priority queues.

A limited number of transmit buffers has been discussed in [6,11,5,12,13]. In [6] the authors compared two CAN communication controllers (Intel 82527 and Philips 82C200). They showed that a significant and unbounded priority inversion can occur for the case of a single transmit buffer with buffer preemption, where the buffering overhead prevents a message refilling a transmit buffer to take part in the next arbitration round. In [11] the authors addressed the availability of multiple (but limited) transmit buffers, and its effect on priority inversion due to buffer preemption.

Di Natale [5] presents the WCRT analysis for CAN communication for the case of a single transmit buffer without buffer preemption when the buffering overhead can be ignored, i.e. when the buffering overhead is less than the inter-frame time, being the time spent between the transmission of two consecutive CAN messages.

In [12] the authors presented a sufficient schedulability analysis for the case of three or more transmit buffers with buffer preemption assuming the buffering overhead cannot be ignored. In a following study, Khan et al. [13] presented a sufficient schedulability analysis for at least three transmit buffers without buffer preemption, ignoring the buffering overhead.

div.head: II. REAL-TIME SCHEDULING MODEL
div.p: In this section we start with describing the general system model. We subsequently present the idealized and a more realistic, communication models for the CAN network.

div.head: A. System model
div.p: An in-vehicle CAN network consists of electronic controller units (ECUs), called nodes, connected via CAN bus. Each node roughly consists of a central processing unit (CPU), memory (RAM, ROM and EEPROM etc.), I/O interface and a communication block. The communication controller and controller-host interface (CHI) form the communication protocol block. The host and the communication controllers are connected by means of a two-way CHI. The communication controller involves a protocol engine that implements the protocol services independent from the applications in the host processor. Protocol services such as transmitting and receiving the messages are implemented by the communication controller. Transmit and receive buffers, i.e. hardware buffers residing in the CAN communication controller, are needed for the transmit and receive operations.

div.head: B. CAN communication model
div.p: In this subsection we first describe the idealized model. Next, we present a more realistic, CAN communication model that is constructed over the idealized model but for the case of a single transmit buffer without buffer preemption.

1) Idealized model: The network is assumed to contain a static set M of m independent hard real-time messages. Each message m i is statically assigned to a node (Node r) on the network and has a fixed and unique priority P 1 , P 2 , ..., P m . For notational convenience messages in a CAN network are assumed to be given in order of decreasing priorities, i.e. m 1 has the highest priority (P 1 ) and m m has the lowest (P m ). For ease of readability an alternative node representation N i is used in the analysis that denotes the transmitter node of the message m i . A message is defined as an infinite stream of invocations. Each message m i is characterized by a (release) period (minimum inter-arrival time) T i ∈ R + , an queueing jitter J i ∈ R + ∪ {0} where J i < T i , a (relative) deadline D i ∈ R + where D i ≤ T i , and a maximum transmission time c i ∈ R + where c i ≤ D i . We assume an arbitrary phasing for messages.
The maximum transmission time c i of message m i can be calculated by
div.formula: c i = lm i × τ bit , (1
div.p: where τ bit represents the 1-bit time in a CAN network which is given by
div.formula: τ bit = 1 Br , (2
div.p: where Br is the data rate (bandwidth) of the CAN bus, e.g. 125 kb/s, 250 kb/s, 500 kb/s and 1 Mb/s. Each message has a hard deadline D i , that is the maximum permitted time from the occurrence of the initiating event to the end of the successful transmission of the message m i .

The worst-case response time WR i of a message is defined as the longest time from the start of the queuing jitter interval of an initiating event until the message m i is received by the nodes that require it. A message is said to be schedulable if and only if its WCRT is less than or equal to its deadline WR i ≤ D i . The network is schedulable if and only if all messages in the system are schedulable.

The ideal model is based on the assumption that all messages to be transmitted can be considered to reside in a single priority-based queue. Figure 1 illustrates the idealized CAN communication model for the transmit operation. The term R i stands for the response time of message m i that is to be transmitted from Node r (or N i ), and th tr i is the amount of time spent by message m i waiting in the priority queue before the start of the transmission, i.e. due to blocking by a lower priority message and interference of higher priority messages from both the same node Node r and the other nodes in the network. The term c i stands for the transmission time of message m i that is calculated using ( 1) and ( 2).

In the ideal model, the hardware and implementation issues such as the limited number of transmit buffers, the buffering overhead and buffer preemption are not considered. These will be explained in the following section.

2) A more realistic model: When a CAN message is released and in case there is an available, i.e. unoccupied, hardware transmit buffer, the message is written to that transmit buffer ready to be transmitted. Otherwise, the message is stored in a priority-based software queue in the host controller (CPU). If a transmit buffer becomes free, the highest priority message among the messages awaiting in the software queue is written to the transmit buffer, and the message starts waiting to be transmitted. The release time of a message is assumed to be the time instant at which the message is ready to be written to the transmit buffer, i.e. the buffering operation. The operations involving a release time of a message, such as the preparation of the message and storing the message in the software queue, are assumed to be part of the computation time of the task sending the message. Similar to the software queue, the transmit buffers are assumed to be priority based, i.e. the highest priority message in a transmit buffer of a node, takes place in the arbitration for the bus.
Three issues that have affect on the response-time of a message should also be discussed: (i) the number of transmit buffers, (ii) buffer preemption, and (iii) buffering overhead.

These issues are independent from each other. The transmission of a message, starting from the release of the message until the completion of the transmission is shown in Figure 2. The response time R i of message m i is the time between the start of the queuing jitter interval and the completion of the successful transmission of that message.

After the generation of message m i , two different paths for buffering the message into a transmit buffer in the communication controller are represented as explained before. Note that buffer preemption is not considered in the figure. In Figure 2 can be greater than zero due to the interference of the higher priority messages m j with j < k ∧ N k = N j .

The term th tr i is the total waiting time of message m i both in the software queue and in the transmit buffer until the start of the transmission of m i . The transmission complete time t tr i is defined as the length of the interval starting at the time message m i is queued in the software queue and ending at the completion of the transmission.

The hardware and implementation issues should be defined clearly to develop a proper schedulability analysis for a CAN network. For example in [5], the CAN communication controller is assumed to have a single message transmit buffer without buffer preemption, e.g. Philips SJA1000. It is also assumed that the buffering overhead (t buff er ) is less than the inter-frame time on the CAN bus and can therefore be ignored, i.e. a message, awaiting in the software queue to be written to the transmit buffer, cannot be blocked by a lower priority message from another node during the buffering time. Moreover, important to mention that if the transmit buffer has already been occupied by a message m j , the buffering of another message m i , which is from the same node and waiting for m j to complete its transmission, is assumed to be done when the transmission of inter-frame bits start.

div.head: III. EXISTING ANALYSIS RECAPITULATED
div.p: In this section we recapitulate the sufficient schedulability analysis presented in [3] for the idealized communication model. Next, we recapitulate the WCRT analysis in [5] that addresses the case of a single transmit buffer without buffer preemption when the buffering overhead can be ignored. IV. THE EXISTING ANALYSIS [5] REVISITED The analysis presented in [5] is based on the extended communication model given in Section II with the specified hardware/implementation properties. In this section, the analysis is revisited by means of an example message set.

We consider a simple two-node CAN network, with timing and priority characteristics of a message set M I [3] as given in Table I. For the following and the other examples in the paper, in case not specified, all timing values such as T i , D i , c i and J i are given in milliseconds (ms), and the data rate Br of the CAN bus is assumed to be 125 kb/s, which yields τ bit = 8 µs by (2). Assuming 11-bit identifiers, the maximum length of each message is 125 bits. We find the WCRT of m 3 , WR 3 = 3 by applying the analysis of [5] as presented in Section III-B. If we apply timeline analysis as shown in Figure 3 for m 3 we find WR 3 = 3.5 that is the WCRT of the second instance of m 3 . The system is therefore unschedulable contrary to the WCRT analysis presented in [5]. The analysis in [5] gives optimistic result for m 3 since it only considers the first instance of m 3 .

div.head: V. REVISED ANALYSIS FOR ONE TRANSMIT BUFFER WITHOUT BUFFER PREEMPTION
div.p: To remove the optimism from the analysis in [5], we have to extend the blocking terms of message m i in a similar way as was done in the sufficient analysis for the ideal model of CAN [3]. Similar to the latter analysis, we also include τ bit in the numerator of the fractions. Next to these two modifications, we also revise the analysis at other places.

div.head: A. Only message of a node
div.p: Equation ( 8) for the worst-case blocking B i of a message m i by messages of other nodes remains the same.

div.formula: x = max(B i , c i ) + ∑ k<i ∧ Ni =Nk x + τ bit + J k T k c k . (15

When a lower priority message m j of the same node occupies the transmit buffer, it may experience interference from higher priority messages of other nodes. div.head: E. An example
div.p: The analysis is applied to the following example message set, constructed by us, M II with the characteristics given in Table II, where the letters "e" and "s" near [3] represent the exact and sufficient CAN schedulability analysis respectively. We determine WR 3 by using the analysis described above, and find WR 3 = 9. Figure 4 shows a timeline analysis for WR 3 , and we see that WR 3 = 8. The analysis in [5] gives WR 3 = 7 instead of 8, which is optimistic. Similarly, WR 7 = 8 is also optimistic that can be found as 9 by timeline analysis.

div.head: VI. EVALUATION OF SAE BENCHMARK
div.p: We apply the CAN analysis presented in [3], [5] and this paper to the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) benchmark message set of which properties are given in [14] and [5]. The benchmark consists of 53 periodic and sporadic real-time signals. In [14] the signals in the entire set are packed, and reduced into 17 periodic CAN messages. In this evaluation all time values are in milliseconds for the bus data rate of 250 kb/s that yields τ bit = 4 µs.
Figure 5 compares the WCRT values based on three different schedulability analyses.

As observed from the graph the analysis in [5] outputs smaller results for the messages m 15 and m 17 compared to [3]. Moreover, it gives smaller results compared to our analysis except for the messages m 2 , m 3 , m 4 , m 5 , m 11 and m 14 . In general, comparatively the revised analysis, presented in Section V, gives more pessimistic results. The exact WCRT values can be obtained by performing timeline analysis. VII. CONCLUSION Controller area network (CAN) is mainly used in safety-critical realtime applications that have strict timing requirements in communication, i.e. the hard real-time message traffic on the CAN bus. The communication schedulability analysis of such networks play an important role in the design and implementation of these applications.

In this paper, we addressed the CAN schedulability analysis for the case of a single transmit buffer without buffer preemption assuming that the buffering overhead can be ignored. We revisited the existing worst-case response-time analysis given in [5], and we showed that the analysis is optimistic. Moreover, we presented a revised analysis for this case. This revision turns out to be non-trivial when a message is neither the only nor the lowest priority message send by a node. The schedulability analysis for the case of a single transmit buffer without buffer preemption assuming that the buffering overhead cannot be ignored and the generalization of the analysis for the case of multiple buffers are left as future work.
